doc.$comment: The representation rules: which way of showing a collection fits which task and data shape. This is the 'Choosing between neighbours' section of AGENTS.md made machine-readable, consolidated from NN/g (data tables, cards, dashboards), uxpatterns.dev, Smart Interface Design Patterns, Pencil & Paper and SAP Fiori floorplans. check-screen-spec.mjs enforces it: a zone that declares its task and data shape may only use a representation some matching rule chooses. The division of labour is deliberate: the spec author (human or agent) names the task and the data, which is a judgment the reviewer approves; this file decides what that judgment permits, which is a computation. Sources and the audit behind every rule: the 2026-08-20 UX decision layer audit (memory: project-ux-decision-layer).

overview.useWhen: The entry point of a domain: a glance across two or more sources, and the action itself happens in the places you navigate to.
overview.notWhen: One data source, or the work happens here — that is a list or a detail.

list.useWhen: Find and act: search, filter and sort a large set to locate the items worth acting on.
list.notWhen: The queue is given and needs processing (worklist), or the items are destinations (hub).
list.expectsNote: a list archetype usually narrows, and nothing here searches or filters — if the queue is given, the archetype is "worklist"

worklist.useWhen: Work through a given queue: every item needs a decision or a completion, and nobody goes looking for items.
worklist.notWhen: The user still has to find the relevant items first — that is a list.
worklist.forbidBecause: a worklist processes a given queue — a FilterBar means the user still has to find, which is the "list" archetype (Fiori: worklist = list report minus the filter bar)

analytical.useWhen: One investigation loop: aggregate on top, the transactional rows under it, acted on where they are.
analytical.notWhen: Pure monitoring (overview) or a plain transaction list (list).

detail.useWhen: One record in full: read it, decide about it, occasionally edit it, in sections.
detail.notWhen: Several records at once, or a guided first-time creation (wizard).

wizard.useWhen: A long or unfamiliar creation task, split into sequential revealed steps with a summary at the end.
wizard.notWhen: Two steps, or a routine the user already knows — a wizard there only adds clicks (Fiori).

form.useWhen: A capture: fields the user fills in and commits. Which KIND of form (dialog, panel, page, draft, settings, …) is the next decision down, and screen-specs/form-rules.json computes it from the field count, the familiarity, the context and the commit model.
form.notWhen: Long AND unfamiliar (wizard), or public users under load — they get one thing per page (GOV.UK).

auth.useWhen: Sign in or sign up: minimal distraction, guarded error copy.
auth.notWhen: Anything else — an auth page that also lists or explains is two screens.

hub.useWhen: Entry points to other places: one tile per destination, saying what waits inside it.
hub.notWhen: The items are records to find or process rather than places to go.

settings.useWhen: Configuration read rarely and changed deliberately: grouped sections of explained knobs — every row says what it actually affects — found by scanning labels, not by searching.
settings.notWhen: The 'settings' are really a collection to manage (members, keys as records) — that is a list; or one preference living beside the work it affects, which stays on that screen.

system.useWhen: The screens around the product: empty start, 404, service unavailable, interruption.
system.notWhen: A state a real screen should carry itself (every list already owes its own empty state).

grid.means: virtualized table: unbounded rows, Excel-like manipulation. The ARIA grid pattern comes with it: one tab stop, arrow keys between cells, Home and End.

table.means: columns over rows: side-by-side comparison, sort and filter by field. WHICH KIND of table (list, worklist, selection, analytical, pivot, comparison, tree, schedule, diff, …) is the next decision down, and screen-specs/table-rules.json computes it from what a row is, what the reader does, how many rows there are and whether a cell interacts.

list.means: one row per item, few attributes, linear scanning

stats.means: KPI tiles and gauges: values read at a glance

cards.means: self-contained tiles: each item read and judged on its own

rules.title: Looking up and comparing records wants columns
rules.because: Two adjacent data points in a column are compared without moving the eyes or holding values in working memory; cards force spatial reorientation per item and de-emphasize ranking (NN/g data tables, NN/g cards).
rules.good: …10 sortable columns……
rules.bad: a Card per user with ten MetaItems — comparing two users now means reading two paragraphs

rules.title: Editing at scale is a data grid
rules.because: When cell-level editing is the primary task the surface is a data grid; a plain table carries occasional inline edits only (Smart Interface Design Patterns).
rules.good: <DataGrid> with editable cells
rules.bad: a Card per row with an Edit dialog behind every field

rules.title: Scanning a few attributes wants rows
rules.because: With one to three attributes per item a linear list scans fastest; columns earn their chrome only when several fields are compared (uxpatterns.dev: start with list).
rules.good: <ListItem> title + one meta line + trailing action
rules.bad: a three-column Table whose header row labels the obvious

rules.title: Judging candidates one by one wants tiles
rules.because: Browsing has no single target: each item is read and judged on its own content, so it gets a self-contained surface. The moment the job becomes comparing fields across items, the task is compare and R1 applies (NN/g cards: browsing, not searching).
rules.good: <Card stretch> per team: name, score Badge, the reasons as sentences
rules.bad: a Table whose cells hold sentences — comparison across rows of prose compares nothing

rules.title: Monitoring wants preattentive values
rules.because: A monitoring surface is read at a glance and acted on elsewhere: encode quantity with length and position (Stat, Meter), never with prose or rows (NN/g dashboards).
rules.good: <Stat size=lg> beside a <Meter> with a target marker
rules.bad: a Table of KPI names and numbers that has to be read line by line

rules.title: Analysis drills from aggregate to rows
rules.because: Analysis is one investigation loop: the aggregate on top, the transactional rows under it, acted on where they are (SAP Fiori analytical list page).
rules.good: Stat row above the Table it summarises
rules.bad: the aggregate on one screen and the rows behind a navigation

rules.title: Prose is never tabular
rules.because: A collection of text-heavy items (questions, messages, findings) is read item by item; a table of paragraphs has columns that align nothing (NN/g data tables: tables are for discrete comparable values).
rules.good: <Card stretch> per question: who asked, the text, the answer, the actions
rules.bad: <Table> with a 'Question' column four lines tall

rules.title: A queue is a worklist
rules.because: Working through items that each need a decision is a worklist: the set is given, so it needs density and status, not discovery chrome (SAP Fiori worklist = list report minus the filter bar).
rules.good: <Table> of items with a status Badge and one action per row
rules.bad: a card grid the user has to graze over to find what is next

rules.title: A short queue reads as cards
rules.because: R8's density argument is about SCALE: with a handful of items, per-item actions and reading beat column density. Two live precedents: the DS ForReview queue (approve / request changes on each card) and a real risk board. At cardinality many, R8 alone applies and cards fail again.
rules.good: <Card tight> per item: eyebrow, title, meta, two small actions
rules.bad: a three-row Table whose header chrome outweighs its rows

rules.title: Entry points are tiles
rules.because: A hub's items are destinations, not records: a tile per destination with what is waiting inside it (SAP Fiori overview page; LinkTile exists for exactly this).
rules.good: <LinkTile> per chat: topic, what is waiting, when it arrived
rules.bad: a Table of destinations with sortable columns nobody sorts

hard.because: Table renders a known number of rows; an unbounded set is DataGrid, which virtualizes (AGENTS.md: choosing between neighbours).
Editing as the primary task across a collection needs cells, not a dialog behind every card (Smart Interface Design Patterns).

notes.say: three fields rarely earn columns — a list scans faster (uxpatterns.dev); keep the table only if column sorting is really used

a view switcher (rows | cards | table over the SAME collection) is the exception, not the default: offer it only when the collection is both VISUAL (the media identifies the item) and COMPARABLE (fields worth columns) — files, media, products; otherwise fix the one representation these rules chose. When offered: an icon SegmentedControl at the toolbar's trailing edge, the rules' choice as the default, the choice remembered per collection, and every view truncating the same ordered field list rather than inventing its own (Fiori list report, SharePoint views, NN/g). The live reference is the showcase's content-patterns screen.

a worklist's READING ORDER IS ITS PRIORITY ORDER: sortable headers (Th sortable/onSort) hand the ranking back to the user and un-decide what the screen decided. Keep headers static; re-sorting is the `list`/`compare` archetypes' tool. Codified 2026-08-21 from the judge lane's first live catch — a fully conformant queue with sortable columns that only the rubric failed.

layers.means: Which card family, once the answer is cards

doc.$comment: The layer under selection-rules.json. Those rules answer WHICH REPRESENTATION a zone gets — table, list, cards, grid, stats. This file answers the next question, the one that used to be taste: once the answer is cards, WHICH CARD. A card family is chosen by what the card carries (contentKinds: the content type) and what the reader does with it (the same task verbs), and every family names the parts it may not ship without, the components that build it, and the states it owes. Consolidated 2026-08-22 from SAP Fiori overview-page cards (object, list, table, analytical, timeline, stack, component), Salesforce Lightning cards, IBM Carbon tiles (clickable, selectable, expandable), Atlassian Smart Links (inline / card / embed), Microsoft Adaptive Cards (hero, thumbnail, list, digest, media, people, request), Shopify Polaris (header / body / footer roles), USWDS card variants, Material 3 surface levels, and the promo survey behind the same research. check-screen-spec.mjs enforces it: a zone whose representation is cards must say what it carries and which family it is, and may only use a family some matching rule chooses.

entity.means: A record with fields of its own: an order, a team, a document, a user.
entity.test: It has an id somewhere and a page it can be opened on.

person.means: A human as the subject: face, role, ways to reach them.
person.test: Replacing the portrait with a field label loses the point of the card.

metric.means: A number on a scale, read for its level and its direction.
metric.test: The reader asks 'is that good?', not 'what is it?'.

request.means: Something waiting for THIS reader's decision or input.
request.test: Doing nothing is itself an outcome someone is waiting on.

event.means: Something that happens at a time: a session, a webinar, a deadline.
event.test: The date is the first thing the reader looks for.

story.means: Prose with a picture: an article, a post, a case write-up.
story.test: The item is read, not compared.

media.means: A recording, a video, a board, a document preview: the frame is the content.
media.test: The card's job is to start playback or open the thing, not to describe it.

destination.means: A place to go rather than a record to read.
destination.test: The card says what is waiting inside, not what the item is.

option.means: One choice in a set the reader picks from.
option.test: Choosing one changes what happens next; not choosing blocks the flow.

offer.means: What we give and what it costs: a plan, a promotion, an upgrade.
offer.test: There is a price, a term, or a condition attached.

proof.means: Evidence for a claim: a quote, a customer logo, a result in a number.
proof.test: Removing it weakens an argument rather than losing information.

capability.means: One thing the product can do, named and explained in a line.
capability.test: It belongs to a set of four to six shown together.

progress.means: Something the reader is partway through: a course, a checklist, an onboarding.
progress.test: The card is different on the second visit than on the first.

collection.means: Several items shown INSIDE one card, under a name for the set.
collection.test: The card is the set; the items inside it are not cards.

change.means: What happened since last time: an audit trail, a digest, a history.

eyebrow.means: what kind of thing this is, above the title

title.means: what it is, in the reader's words

media.means: picture, video frame, icon tile or wash

status.means: the state, as a word and a tone

meta.means: secondary facts and the card's own actions, pinned to the foot

excerpt.means: the first sentences, clamped by the layout rather than cut by hand

value.means: the number the card exists for

delta.means: the comparison that makes the number mean something

trend.means: the shape of the number: over time, per category, or as shares of a whole

scale.means: where the value sits between a floor, a target and a ceiling

progress.means: how far through the reader is

rows.means: the items of a set, inside the card

table.means: three columns of comparable values, inside the card

selection.means: the mark that says this one is chosen, on a card that IS the control

person.means: face beside or over name and role

quote.means: the words of someone who is not us, with the attribution that makes them evidence

price.means: what it costs, and per what

date.means: when it happens, as a block the eye finds first

link.means: the whole surface is the way in

states.$comment: What a family owes besides its happy path. A card that has no answer for these three gets them invented per screen, which is how one system grows four empty states.
states.loading: Skeleton in the card's own shape, so the layout does not jump.
states.empty: EmptyState inside the card, saying WHY it is empty and what to do.
states.error: Alert tone="danger" inside the card, with the retry, never a blank surface.

families.name: Object card
families.intent: One record as a summary: what it is, what state it is in, the few fields that decide, one way in.
families.notWhen: Four or more fields are COMPARED across items — that is R1, and columns win.
families.because: Fiori's object card and Salesforce's record card are the same shape for the same reason: the reader is judging one record at a time, and pairs of label and value read faster than sentences.
families.source: SAP Fiori object card; Salesforce Lightning record card

families.name: List card
families.intent: A few items of one kind inside one card, under a name for the set and a way to the full list.
families.notWhen: The set IS the screen — then it is a list page, not a card.
families.because: The card names the set and bounds it; without the name the rows are a list that happens to sit on a surface (Fiori list card).
families.source: SAP Fiori list card; Adaptive Cards list

families.name: Table card
families.intent: A few rows with two or three comparable values each, inside a card.
families.notWhen: More than three columns or more than a handful of rows — that is a table zone of its own.
families.because: Fiori caps the table card at three columns for the same reason a card is a summary: past that it is a table wearing a card.

families.name: Analytical card
families.intent: A value in a shape: over time, or split by a dimension, with the period it covers.
families.notWhen: One number with no shape — that is the kpi family and does not need a chart.
families.because: A chart card without its period and its freshness is a picture, not a measurement (Fiori analytical card). Three forms cover what a card can hold: a value over time beside a number (Sparkline), a measure across categories or over time with its scale (Chart), a whole split into named shares (DonutChart).

families.name: KPI card
families.intent: One number that says whether things are good: the value, what it is compared to, and where it sits against the target.
families.notWhen: The number is not judged, only read — then it is a field of an object card.
families.because: Four layers make a KPI: the label, the value, the comparison and a visual anchor. Without the third the reader cannot tell good from bad, and the card is decoration.

families.name: Status card
families.intent: The state of one thing against its promise: healthy, at risk, breached, and why.
families.notWhen: The state is one field among many — that belongs on the object card.
families.because: A status card exists to be acted on: the tone carries the verdict, the scale carries the distance to it, and the action is in the card because that is where the decision is made.

families.name: Action card
families.intent: A question put to this reader, answered without leaving the surface, and the answer shown in place.
families.notWhen: The decision needs the full record — then the card links to it and the decision happens there.
families.because: Adaptive Cards exist for this shape: the answer is given in the feed and the card then states the outcome, so nobody wonders whether it went through.
families.source: Microsoft Adaptive Cards; Outlook actionable messages

families.name: Timeline card
families.intent: What happened to one thing, in order, with who and when.
families.notWhen: The events belong to many different things — that is a digest.
families.because: One subject, one axis: the timeline card is the audit trail of the record the screen is about (Fiori timeline card).

families.name: Entity preview
families.intent: A pointer to something that lives elsewhere, shown with enough of itself to be recognised.
families.notWhen: The entity is the screen's own subject — it does not need previewing, it needs showing.
families.because: Atlassian ships one entity in three views because how much context a link owes depends on the sentence it sits in, not on the entity. EntityLink carries the inline and card views; HoverCard is the same preview on hover.

families.name: Person card
families.intent: A human as one glance: face, name, role, and the ways to reach them.
families.notWhen: The people are compared by attributes (rate, availability, load) — that is a table.
families.because: The portrait is what identifies the item; a field list of the same facts identifies nobody.
families.source: Adaptive Cards people card; corporate directories

families.name: Stack card
families.intent: Many cards of one kind shown as one, with the count, a way into the pile and — when the pile is a queue — a way to put the top card behind it and work through the rest in place.
families.notWhen: The set is small enough to show — a stack of three hides nothing and costs a click.
families.because: An overview page has room for one card per topic; when a topic has twenty instances the topic keeps its slot and the instances go behind it (Fiori stack card, capped at 20).

families.name: Selectable tile
families.intent: One choice in a set, chosen by clicking the card itself, single or multiple.
families.notWhen: The choice is a short list of words — that is Select, Radio or SegmentedControl, and a grid of tiles is chrome around a radio group.
families.because: Carbon separates selectable tiles from clickable ones because the two look alike and behave nothing alike: one navigates, one changes a value in a form.
families.source: IBM Carbon selectable / radio / multi-select tile

families.name: Entry tile
families.intent: A place to go, saying what is waiting inside it.
families.notWhen: The items are records to find or process — R9 already says a hub's items are destinations, and these are not.
families.because: A destination tile is judged by what is inside it, so the freshness and the count belong on the tile, not behind it.
families.source: SAP Fiori overview page; our own LinkTile

families.name: Expandable card
families.intent: Summary in place, detail on demand, without leaving the screen.
families.notWhen: Every card ends up open — then the detail was never optional and belongs in the card.
families.because: Carbon's expandable tile keeps the grid scannable while letting one item answer a follow-up question in place. The disclosure is <Accordion>, which owns the header semantics and the keyboard; <ExpandButton> is the pill for a rail or a toolbar, not a quiet in-card reveal.

families.name: Embed card
families.intent: The card lends its chrome to content that is not ours: a video, a board, a document.
families.notWhen: We own the content — then it is the media family and keeps our padding.
families.because: Foreign content brings its own aspect ratio and its own padding; the card has to decide whose wins before the first one lands. `CardMedia ratio` is that decision, made once.
families.source: SAP UI5 component card; Atlassian embed

families.name: Checklist card
families.intent: The steps of a first run or a routine, with the state of each and one active action.
families.notWhen: The steps must be done in order and block each other — that is a wizard, a page not a card.
families.because: Shopify's setup guide works because the card holds the whole sequence: progress, state per step, and exactly one thing to do next.

families.name: Digest card
families.intent: What changed in a period, as a few unlike items under one date.
families.notWhen: The items are all of one kind and belong to one subject — that is a timeline card.
families.because: A digest is defined by its watermark: it says what is new since a moment, so the period is part of the card, not a filter above it.

families.name: Plan card
families.intent: One plan in a row: what it is called, what it costs, what is included, one action.
families.notWhen: There is a deadline or a condition rather than a tier — that is the offer family.
families.because: Plans are compared down the row, so every card carries the same fields in the same order; the featured one is marked, not enlarged.

families.name: Cover card
families.intent: The picture is the card: title over the image, legibility from the scrim.
families.notWhen: The picture is decoration — a cover with a stock photograph behind the title costs contrast and buys nothing.
families.because: A cover promises that the image carries part of the meaning; the scrim is what makes the promise keepable over any photograph.

families.name: Story card
families.intent: Picture, headline, the first sentences, one way in.
families.notWhen: The items are compared by fields — prose in columns compares nothing (R7).
families.because: The excerpt is the working part: it is what lets the reader skip the item without opening it. <ContentCard> carries the whole set — media, eyebrow, title, excerpt, meta, actions — and reads its own width, so the same story is a row in a sidebar and a tile in a grid without a second component.
families.source: USWDS card, flag and header-first variants

families.name: Feature tile
families.intent: One thing the product does: icon, name, one line. Lives in a set of four to six.
families.notWhen: The line needs a paragraph — then it is a story card and the set is smaller.
families.because: The set is read as one sentence about the product, so the tiles are parallel in length and grammar or the set stops reading as a set.

families.name: Media card
families.intent: A recording: the frame, how long it runs, and the way to start it.
families.notWhen: Nothing plays — a document with a thumbnail is a story card.
families.because: Duration and the play affordance are what separate a recording from a picture; without them the card lies about what a click does. CardMedia carries both (`playable`, `duration`), so the affordance is one shape across every screen.

families.name: Case card
families.intent: Client, task, result in a number.
families.notWhen: There is no number — an unquantified case is a story card and should not pretend otherwise.
families.because: The number is the whole argument; a case card that buries it in the excerpt is a story with a logo.

families.name: Proof stat
families.intent: One number as an argument, in a row of three or four.
families.notWhen: The number is monitored rather than claimed — that is the kpi family.
families.because: A promotional number needs its source in the card or it reads as a decoration nobody checked.

families.name: Testimonial card
families.intent: The words of someone who used the thing, with who they are.
families.notWhen: The quote has no attributable human — an anonymous testimonial proves nothing and should be cut, not styled.
families.because: Attribution is the evidence; the quote alone is copy we wrote about ourselves.

families.name: Offer card
families.intent: What we give, on what condition, until when, with one action.
families.notWhen: It is a tier in a range — that is the plan family.
families.because: The term is what makes it an offer; without the deadline the card is a plan and should be compared like one.

families.name: Event card
families.intent: When it happens, what it is, where, and how to be there.
families.notWhen: The date is one field among equals — that is an object card.
families.because: Readers scan events by date, so the date is a block the eye lands on, not a line of meta under the title.

families.name: Course card
families.intent: A learning unit: what it is, how long, how far the reader got, continue or start.
families.notWhen: Nobody's progress is stored — then it is a story card with a duration.
families.because: The card is different on the second visit, and that difference is the product: continue is not the same offer as start.

families.name: Comparison card
families.intent: Two columns in one card: before and after, ours and theirs, base and extended.
families.notWhen: More than six rows or more than two columns — that is a table.
families.because: Two columns of six rows is the size at which a card still reads at a glance; past it the card is a table that lost its header.

families.name: Capture card
families.intent: One promise, one field, one button, and the truth about what arrives afterwards.
families.notWhen: More than one field — that is a form, and a form on a promo page is a page.
families.because: The line about frequency is part of the card: it is the only place the reader learns what they are agreeing to.

rules.title: A judged number is a KPI card
rules.because: Monitoring asks whether things are good, which is a comparison: the value alone cannot answer it (NN/g dashboards; BI practice).
rules.good: <Stat value delta="+12%" trend={…}> in a Card
rules.bad: a big number with a label and nothing to judge it against

rules.title: Analysis wants the shape, not the point
rules.because: An investigation starts from the curve; the single value is the headline of a chart that has to be there (Fiori analytical list page).
rules.good: Card with a Sparkline over the period and the value beside it
rules.bad: one number per period as separate Stat tiles

rules.title: A record read one at a time is an object card
rules.because: Label and value pairs are what let a reader judge one record without the header row of a table (Fiori object card).
rules.good: Card with a Descriptions of four fields and one action
rules.bad: a Card holding ten MetaItems in a paragraph

rules.title: Something waiting on the reader is an action card
rules.because: The answer is given where the question is asked, and the card then states the outcome (Adaptive Cards).
rules.good: <ActionCard> with approve and decline, and a resolved state after either
rules.bad: a card whose only action navigates to the screen where the decision really happens

rules.title: Destinations are entry tiles
rules.because: A hub's item is a place, so the tile carries what is waiting inside it (R9; Fiori overview page).
rules.good: <LinkTile> with the topic, the count and when it last moved
rules.bad: an object card whose fields describe a page rather than a record

rules.title: Prose with a picture is a story
rules.because: A text item is read and judged on its own content (R7), and the excerpt is what lets it be skipped.
rules.good: Card with CardMedia, CardTitle, two sentences and a meta line
rules.bad: a story card with no excerpt, which forces every item open

rules.title: A choice in a set is a selectable tile
rules.because: Selecting changes a value in a flow, so the whole surface is the control and its state has to be visible (Carbon selectable tile).
rules.good: <SelectableTile> per region with a checked state and keyboard support
rules.bad: a clickable card that navigates when the user meant to choose

rules.title: A set inside a card is a list card
rules.because: The card names the set and bounds it, which is what separates it from a list that happens to sit on a surface (Fiori list card).
rules.good: Card titled 'Waiting on you' over five ListItems and a way to the full list
rules.bad: a card with twenty rows and no way out of it

rules.title: What changed is a digest or a history
rules.because: Time is the axis: one subject in order is a timeline, many subjects since a moment is a digest.
rules.good: Card headed by the period, five unlike items, each with its own way in
rules.bad: a digest with no period, which cannot say what is new

rules.title: A person is a face, not a row of fields
rules.because: The portrait is what identifies the item; the same facts as a field list identify nobody.
rules.good: <Identity vertical size="xl"> in a Card with two named actions
rules.bad: a Descriptions list whose first row is 'Name'

rules.title: Evidence is not an object
rules.because: Proof carries attribution rather than fields: who said it, for whom, measured how.
rules.good: a quote with the person, their role and their company
rules.bad: an unattributed quote styled as a testimonial

rules.title: An offer is a plan plus a term
rules.because: Tiers are compared across the row; an offer is judged against its deadline. Same surface, different reading.
rules.good: <PlanCard> for the range, an offer card for the campaign
rules.bad: a promotional card in the pricing row that cannot be compared with its neighbours

rules.title: The date leads an event
rules.because: Readers scan an event list by date, so the date is a block, not a line of meta.
rules.good: a date block beside the title, place and time under it, one action
rules.bad: the date as the fourth MetaItem in the footer

rules.title: Progress changes the offer
rules.because: Continue and start are different promises; the card has to know which one it is making.
rules.good: Card with a ProgressBar and a Continue button when there is progress
rules.bad: the same Start button whether or not the reader is halfway through

rules.title: Playable media says so
rules.because: Duration and the play affordance are what tell the reader what a click does.
rules.good: a frame with a play control and a duration badge
rules.bad: a thumbnail that opens a player nobody expected

rules.title: A capability is one line
rules.because: The set of tiles is read as one sentence about the product, so the tiles stay parallel in length and grammar.
rules.good: four tiles, each an icon, a two-word name and one line
rules.bad: one tile with a paragraph and three with a phrase

hard.because: A card that carries a decision and only links away hands the work back to the reader; the answer belongs where the question is (Adaptive Cards).
A clickable card navigates and a selectable one changes a value; using the first for the second loses the choice on the next click (Carbon).
One measured value is a KPI card; wrapping it in a set of rows buries the only thing on the card.

notes.say: every card family owes three states besides its happy path: Skeleton in its own shape while loading, EmptyState with the reason when there is nothing, Alert tone="danger" with the retry when it broke. A screen that invents them per card is how one system grows four empty states.

cards in a row are the SAME HEIGHT (owner's rule, 23.08). The grid stretches them by default and that default stays: a card that runs out of content gives the extra height to the space above its foot, because CardMeta pins to the bottom. Do not answer a ragged row with `align="start"`; answer it by giving the short card the part it is missing. `fill` is how a card takes its cell's height when something (a GridItem, a flex row) sits between it and the grid.
one primary way in per card. A card that is itself a link (Card interactive) may not also carry a primary Button — the two compete for the same click and the nested one usually loses.

doc.$componentsNote: A family's components say what it is BUILT from: `required` must all be named by the zone, `oneOf` means at least one of them (the purpose-built component or the honest composition), `expect` is a note rather than a verdict — the part that has a component nobody remembered to use. `optional` is documentation.

layers.means: Which kind of form a zone that takes input is

doc.$comment: The form decision layer. selection-rules.json answers WHICH REPRESENTATION a collection gets and card-rules.json answers WHICH CARD once the answer is cards; this file answers the question that used to be taste on the other side of the screen: once a zone CAPTURES INPUT, which kind of form it is, what it is built from, and how it commits. A kind is chosen by four things and nothing else: how many fields, how familiar the task is, whether the surrounding context has to stay visible, and who commits the change. Consolidated 2026-08-23 from GOV.UK (question pages, one thing per page, error summary, conditional reveal, marking the minority), SAP Fiori (object page create/edit mode, footer bar, draft handling), Baymard (label placement, inline validation timing), NN/g and GitLab Pajamas (saving and feedback), Carbon and Polaris (form structure), and WCAG 2.2 (1.3.5, 3.3.1, 3.3.7, 3.3.8). The survey behind it is docs/RESEARCH-FORMS.md. check-screen-spec.mjs enforces it: a zone whose task is input must say which kind of form it is and how it commits, and may only use a kind some matching rule chooses.

explicit.means: The user presses a named button and the record changes then, not before.
explicit.use: Records: anything another person or another screen reads afterwards.

per-row.means: Each control applies on change, on its own, with its own feedback.
per-row.use: Settings: knobs read rarely and changed one at a time.

autosave.means: The form saves itself after a pause in typing and states when it last did.
autosave.use: Drafts: long, resumable work where 'continue later' is expected.

none.means: Nothing is committed at all: the input narrows or searches what is already there.
none.use: Filters and search. They own no Save, no dirty state and no error summary.

standalone.means: The form is the screen. Nothing behind it needs reading.

over-list.means: Opened from a collection the user was working in.

beside-context.means: The record, list or document behind it must stay readable while the fields are filled in.

in-place.means: The field is edited where it is read, inside other content.

dialog.means: A modal form over the screen that opened it.
dialog.useWhen: 1 to 6 fields, routine, reversible, and the list behind it is the context.
dialog.notWhen: The record has named sections, or the page behind it has to be read while typing.
owes: A primary that names the event, never 'Submit'.
Every field reachable without the dialog scrolling past its own actions.

panel.means: The same form in a side panel, with the context still on screen.
panel.useWhen: Editing while the record or the list behind it stays readable.
panel.notWhen: The form is longer than the panel scrolls comfortably, or nothing behind it matters.
owes: The panel keeps its own footer actions; the page's actions stay for the page.

page.means: A page-sized form: sections under a header, actions in a footer bar.
page.useWhen: 7 or more fields, or the form has named sections, or the form IS the screen's job.
page.notWhen: Three fields, which a dialog does without a route change; or an unfamiliar sequence, which is a wizard.
owes: Sections with real legends once there is more than one group.
An error summary above the first field on a failed submit.
Actions pinned in the footer bar, reachable without scrolling to the end.

wizard.means: One sequential task split into revealed steps, with a check-answers step at the end.
wizard.useWhen: Long AND unfamiliar, order matters, and a summary is owed before the commit.
wizard.notWhen: Two steps, or a routine the user repeats: a wizard there is a page form with extra clicks (Fiori).
owes: A review step that repeats every answer with a Change link (WCAG 3.3.7: never ask twice).
Steps addressable in the URL, so a reload does not restart the task.

question.means: One question per screen, Continue underneath.
question.useWhen: Public or infrequent users, branching questions, low confidence, or a flow that must survive being abandoned (GOV.UK one thing per page).
question.notWhen: Internal users who repeat the flow daily: they pay for it in clicks.
owes: Its own URL per question, so back and bookmark both work.
question.waitingFor: a public-facing flow in one of the products; internal screens have never needed it
question.note: Was `planned` with no `opensWhen` — a claim with no expiry, which is how a status outlives the thing it described. Marked built on 2026-08-26 when a specimen was written for it out of registry parts only. Composable today from a heading and two Buttons; the kind is a LAYOUT decision (one question per screen), not a part the system was missing.

review.means: Every answer restated before an irreversible commit, each with a link back to where it was given.
review.useWhen: The submit cannot be taken back, or the user has been away between steps.
review.notWhen: Nothing is irreversible and the whole form is on one screen anyway.
owes: Change links whose accessible name carries the field, not five bare 'Change' links.

settings.means: Grouped sections of explained knobs, each applied on its own.
settings.useWhen: Configuration read rarely and changed deliberately; every row says what it actually affects.
settings.notWhen: The rows are really records to manage, which is a list.
owes: No page-level Save: a page that applies some rows and asks for Save on others is a page nobody trusts.

auth.means: Sign in, sign up, reset, verify.
auth.useWhen: The screen's only job is identifying the user.
auth.notWhen: Anything with a second purpose on the same screen.
owes: Paste into the password field stays allowed and the browser may fill it (WCAG 3.3.8).
Error copy that does not say which half of the pair was wrong.

inline.means: One field edited where it is read.
inline.useWhen: A single value on a record the user is already looking at: a title, an owner, a status.
inline.notWhen: Several fields at once, which is a panel or a dialog.
owes: The read and edit states occupy the same space, so nothing below moves when editing starts.
inline.waitingFor: a second product asking for it; RenameDialog covers the one live case
inline.note: Was `planned` with no `opensWhen` — a claim with no expiry, which is how a status outlives the thing it described. Marked built on 2026-08-26 when a specimen was written for it out of registry parts only. <InlineText> is the part, and it has been in the registry since before this status was written.

bulk.means: One change applied to the records the user selected.
bulk.useWhen: The same edit across many rows, with the count stated in the copy.
bulk.notWhen: The change differs per record: that is editing each one.
owes: The number of records in the confirm copy, and what happens to the ones that fail.
bulk.waitingFor: a product with a selection model in a list
bulk.note: Was `planned` with no `opensWhen` — a claim with no expiry, which is how a status outlives the thing it described. Marked built on 2026-08-26 when a specimen was written for it out of registry parts only. <BatchActions> states the count and <Modal actions> asks the question; both exist.

grid.means: Editing across a collection, in the cells themselves.
grid.useWhen: Editing many records is the primary task.
owes: A row that fails says so in the row, not in a dialog about the whole grid.

confirm.means: Yes or no on a stated consequence.
confirm.useWhen: A destructive or irreversible action needs an explicit second press.
confirm.notWhen: The user has to type anything: that is a verified confirm.
owes: The consequence in the copy, and the real verb on the button.

verified-confirm.means: A destructive action gated behind typing the thing's own name.
verified-confirm.useWhen: Unrecoverable and wide: deleting a workspace, revoking everyone's access.
verified-confirm.notWhen: Recoverable actions, where typing is theatre and trains people to type through warnings.
owes: The exact string to type, quoted, and a primary that stays inert until it matches.
verified-confirm.waitingFor: a product with an unrecoverable, wide-blast-radius action
verified-confirm.note: Was `planned` with no `opensWhen` — a claim with no expiry, which is how a status outlives the thing it described. Marked built on 2026-08-26 when a specimen was written for it out of registry parts only. <Modal> takes children and `actions.confirmDisabled`, so the field and the armed button are one dialog. This is the same unblocking as lifecycle-rules' `confirm-typed` on the same day: the blocker was that no dialog both took input and coloured its commitment, and folding FormModal into Modal made one that does.

upload.means: Files plus the metadata that describes them.
upload.useWhen: What is being captured IS the file, and the fields explain it.
upload.notWhen: Files alone with nothing to say about them: that is the control, not a form.
owes: Progress per file, and a failure that names the file rather than the batch.

draft.means: A long form that saves itself and can be left.
draft.useWhen: Resumable work where 'continue later' is expected and losing it is the real risk.
draft.notWhen: Short forms: autosave there surprises more than it helps.
owes: A status line that says when it last saved, and what happens when a save fails.

composer.means: Free text plus attachments, sent rather than saved.
composer.useWhen: The result is a message in a thread.
composer.notWhen: The result is a record with fields.
owes: Enter sends or Enter breaks the line, decided once and stated.

filter.means: Input that narrows a collection already on screen.
filter.useWhen: Nothing is committed: the values change what is shown, and are gone next time unless the screen remembers them.
filter.notWhen: The values persist as a record: that is a real form.
owes: A way to clear everything, and the current narrowing visible without opening a menu.

search.means: One query field, submitted to find.
search.notWhen: More than one criterion, which is a filter.
owes: An empty result that says what was searched for.

rules.because: Up to eight routine fields opened from a list is a dialog: the list is the context, and a route change to a page loses it. Past that the dialog scrolls its own actions off screen (HF1).
When the thing behind the form has to stay readable, a modal is the wrong container: it covers exactly what the user is copying from.

Past six fields a dialog scrolls its own actions off screen and has nowhere to put sections (Fiori: create page, not create dialog). Steps are not automatic here: they are earned by unfamiliarity (F4), not by length.
Long AND unfamiliar is the one case steps earn their clicks: the user cannot judge the whole form at once, so it is revealed a step at a time.
Long but familiar is a page form. Forcing steps on a routine the user repeats weekly only adds clicks (Fiori).
Public users under load do better with one thing per page: it survives interruption, branches cleanly and handles errors one at a time (GOV.UK).
Applying each control on its own IS the settings model; anything else with a per-row commit is a settings screen that has not admitted it.
Autosave belongs to work that is long enough to lose. A short form that saves itself leaves the user unsure anything happened.
Input that commits nothing is a narrowing, not a form: no Save, no dirty state, no error summary.
One value on a record already on screen is edited where it is read; opening a dialog for it costs more than the edit.

A form with no fields of its own is a decision, not a capture: it asks yes or no, asks the user to type the name of what they are destroying, or restates the answers already given before an irreversible submit.
A short standalone capture is a page form or one of the specialised short screens; which one is decided by what it captures, not by its length.

hard.because: Nine or more fields in a dialog scroll the actions out of the viewport and leave sections nowhere to go (Fiori: create page).
A container with Cancel in its footer promises the change can be abandoned; autosave has already committed it.
A screen that commits nothing must not carry a Save: it teaches the user that Save sometimes means nothing.
Mixing per-row apply with a page-level Save on one screen is the save model nobody can predict (Pajamas: do not mix).

notes.say: four or more fields committed at once: a failed submit owes an <ErrorSummary> above the first field, focused, with a row per failure — marking fields in place only helps someone who can see the whole form at once (GOV.UK)
eight or more fields read as one undifferentiated column: group them into <FormSection>s whose legends say who or what each group is about, or split the form into steps
an autosaving form owes a <SaveStatus>: without it the user invents their own proof that the work is safe, usually by retyping it
a public audience on one long page is the case GOV.UK measured as failing: low-confidence users do better with one question per screen, and the flow survives being abandoned
a wizard's last step is a check-answers step (<WizardReview>): re-asking what was already answered is the WCAG 2.2 redundant-entry failure, and the summary is where it is usually broken

layers.means: Which control one field gets, from what the value takes

$comment: WHICH CONTROL A VALUE GETS — the layer under form-rules.json.
form-rules decides what KIND of form a zone is: a dialog, a panel, a page, a
wizard. It names the parts that build the container and stops there. Nothing
in this system has ever said when a field is a Slider and when it is a
NumberInput, when a boolean is a Switch and when it is a Checkbox, or at how
many options a Radio group becomes a Select.
That gap was measured rather than felt (2026-08-31): eight of the thirteen
components no rule and no product named were input controls — DatePicker,
DateRangePicker, Slider, RangeSlider, TagInput, CodeInput, InputGroup,
ConditionalReveal. They were not unused because they were wrong. They were
unused because nothing in the system could say when to reach for them, so
every screen that needed one either hand-rolled it or picked the nearest
A zone that takes input may declare `controls`, the same way a table zone
declares `columns`. Each control names what it TAKES, and the kind decides
the component and what it owes. `data.fields` stays what it was: a count,
which is what form-rules reads to choose dialog against page against wizard.
This layer is about each field; that one is about how many there are.
Every component named below is in the registry and is built.

text.means: One line of free text: a name, a reference, a title.
text.useWhen: The value is short, and the reader writes it rather than picks it.
text.notWhen: The set of acceptable answers is known — that is a choice, not typing.
owes: A label that names the value, not the action: "Supplier", not "Enter supplier".
The browser's own purpose where it has one (autocomplete), so a phone fills it in.

long-text.means: Several sentences: a note, a description, a reason.
long-text.useWhen: The answer is prose and its length is not known in advance.
long-text.notWhen: One line is the honest expectation — a tall box asks for an essay.
owes: A capped field says what is left, under it, as it is typed (<CharacterCount>).
Room for the answer it expects: a box sized for one line teaches the reader to write one.

number.means: A quantity typed exactly: how many, how long, how far.
number.useWhen: The digits are the point and the reader knows them.
number.notWhen: The value is a position on a scale — see `bounded`.
owes: A step that matches the quantity: a whole number of people steps by one, not by 0.1.
Tabular figures, so a column of them lines up.

amount.means: A number that is nothing without its unit: a price, a weight, a rate.
amount.useWhen: The unit is fixed by the screen rather than chosen by the reader.
amount.notWhen: The reader picks the unit too — that is two controls, and the unit is a `choice`.
owes: The unit attached to the field, never only in the label: a value read back without its unit is a different value.
The unit on the side the language puts it: a currency leads, a weight trails.

bounded.means: A position on a known scale, where the digits are not the point.
bounded.useWhen: Both ends are fixed and the reader is choosing more or less, not a figure.
bounded.notWhen: The exact number matters. A slider for a price is a control that cannot be typed.
owes: The current value shown as a number beside the track: a slider with no readout is a guess.
Both ends labelled, so the scale is legible without dragging it.

span.means: A pair on one scale: from and to.
span.useWhen: The reader is narrowing a range and both ends move.
span.notWhen: The pair is two dates — see `date-span`, which has a calendar.
owes: An ordered pair: the ends clamp against each other rather than crossing.
Both values readable at once, because the range IS the value.

choice.means: One of a few named options, all worth showing at once.
choice.useWhen: Two to five options AND comparing them is part of choosing: a plan, a priority, a delivery speed.
choice.notWhen: The reader already knows their answer and is looking it up rather than weighing it — then a menu is faster to skip past, whatever the count.
owes: Every option visible without a press, in a fixed order.
<SegmentedControl> instead when the options are VIEWS of the same thing and switching is instant.

choice-view.means: One of a few options that are VIEWS of the same thing.
choice-view.useWhen: Switching is instant and nothing is submitted: list against board against calendar.
choice-view.notWhen: The options are values the form carries — that is `choice`, and a radio group says so.
owes: The change applied at once, like a switch: a segmented control behind a Save button is a radio group in disguise.
Two to five segments, all readable without truncation, because the set is the control's whole width.

choice-long.useWhen: Up to fifteen options, and the reader is finding a value rather than comparing the set.
choice-long.notWhen: The list is longer than a menu, or the set is worth comparing and small enough to lay out.
owes: The current value visible on the closed control, not just inside the menu.
An order the reader can predict: alphabetical, or the order the domain uses.

choice-searched.means: One of many, found by typing.
choice-searched.useWhen: More than about fifteen options, or a set the screen does not know in advance.
choice-searched.notWhen: The reader cannot be expected to know the words — a menu they can read beats a box they must guess at.
owes: The typed text marked in each result, so the list says why each one is a hit (<Highlight>).
An answer when nothing matches, which is not an empty menu.

choice-visual.means: An option recognised by how it looks rather than by its name.
choice-visual.useWhen: The look IS the value: a colour, a layout, a plan, a theme.
choice-visual.notWhen: The options differ in words. A tile of text is a radio that takes six times the room.
owes: A name as well as the picture: a swatch with no name is unusable to anyone who cannot see it.
A real radio or checkbox underneath, so the group keeps its arrow keys and its value in a form.

choices.means: Several values from a set the screen knows.
choices.useWhen: The reader may pick none, one or many, and the options are worth showing.
choices.notWhen: The reader invents the values — see `tags`.
owes: A group with a name of its own, so the boxes are announced as one question.
<Combobox multiple> instead once the set is long enough to need searching.

tags.means: Several values the reader invents as they go.
tags.useWhen: The set is open: keywords, recipients, labels.
tags.notWhen: The values must come from a known list — that is `choices`, and a free box invites a typo.
owes: Each value removable on its own, without retyping the rest.
One obvious way to commit a value, and the same one every time.

toggle.means: On or off, and it takes effect the moment it is flipped.
toggle.useWhen: A setting: nothing is submitted, the change IS the action.
toggle.notWhen: The value is part of a form the reader submits — see `agreement`.
owes: A label that reads as a state, not as a command: "Weekly digest", not "Turn on digest".
The result visible without a save: a switch that needs a Save button is a checkbox.

agreement.means: A box the reader ticks, whose value is submitted with the form.
agreement.useWhen: Consent, an option, an opt-in — anything the Save button carries.
agreement.notWhen: The change applies at once. That is a `toggle`, and a switch says so.
owes: The whole label clickable, not just the box.
Stated in the positive: a box that means "do not send" is read wrong by everyone in a hurry.

date.useWhen: The reader is choosing a day, and which day it is has context — a weekend, a deadline, next month.
date.notWhen: The date is a birth date the reader knows by heart: typing beats nine clicks back through a calendar.
owes: Typing as well as picking: a calendar-only field is slow for a date the reader already knows.
The format shown, not guessed at.

date-span.useWhen: The two dates are one decision: a stay, a reporting period, a leave request.
date-span.notWhen: The two are independent — then they are two `date` controls with their own labels.
owes: A backwards pair ordered rather than refused.
The band between the ends painted, because the span is what is being chosen.

time.useWhen: The value is a clock time, with or without a date beside it.
time.notWhen: The value is a duration. A duration is a `number` with a unit.
owes: `type="time"`, so the platform's own clock and keyboard arrive with it.
One zone said, when the screen has more than one.

file.means: One or more files from the reader's machine.
file.useWhen: The value is a document, an image, an export.
file.notWhen: The reader would paste the content — a text box is faster than a round trip through disk.
owes: What is accepted and how large, said before the reader picks, not after.
Each chosen file removable, and the progress of each one visible.

secret.useWhen: The value must not be read over the reader's shoulder.
secret.notWhen: Never anything else: a secret in a plain field is a secret on a screen.
owes: A way to reveal it, because a password typed blind is a password typed wrong.
Never written to storage, and never carried in a URL.

code.means: A short verification code, one box per character.
code.useWhen: A code arrived by mail or by phone and is about to be typed once.
code.notWhen: The value is long or is remembered — one field is kinder than eight.
owes: A paste of the whole code filling every box, because that is how a code arrives.
`autocomplete="one-time-code"`, so the platform offers it.

score.means: A rating out of a fixed number.
score.useWhen: The reader is scoring something and the scale is small and familiar.
score.notWhen: The scale is a measurement — that is `bounded`, and it has a readout.
owes: The value in words as well as in marks, for anyone who cannot see the stars.
A way back to no score, if no score is a legal answer.

query.means: Free text that narrows what is already on screen.
query.useWhen: The typing changes a list rather than filling in a record.
query.notWhen: The text is a value that gets saved. That is `text`, and it belongs in a Field.
owes: No Field and no label above it: the placeholder says what is searched, and the results say the rest.
A way to clear it that does not need selecting the text first.

message.useWhen: The zone is a conversation and the answer goes off immediately.
message.notWhen: The text is saved with everything else on the screen — that is `long-text`.
owes: A send that is reachable from the keyboard, and a stop while the answer is coming.
The box growing with the message, up to a stated limit.

dependent.means: A field that exists only while another control has a particular value.
dependent.useWhen: "Other" needs a box, a plan needs a seat count, a reason needs saying.
dependent.notWhen: The field always applies. A field that appears for everyone is a field that should have been there.
owes: Rendered under the option it belongs to, so the connection is spatial and not remembered.
Its value dropped when the option it depends on is unchosen, so a hidden field cannot be submitted.

rules.title: A control that carries a value lives in a Field
rules.because: The label, the description and the error message are one part in this system, tied to the control by id. Written by hand they drift: the label stops being clickable, the error stops being announced, and the message ends up beside a control a screen reader never connects it to. The three exceptions carry their own name — a search box says what it searches in its placeholder, a composer is the whole zone, and a switch is labelled by the setting it is.

rules.title: A set that cannot be scanned is not laid out, and one that cannot be scrolled is not a menu
rules.because: Two bounds, not three buckets. Laying options out stops working past about five, and a menu stops working past about fifteen — those are the two failures worth a gate. Between them the screen decides, because the real question is whether COMPARING the options is part of choosing: a plan is weighed, an area is looked up. The first cut of this rule made the count pick the kind and failed the admin portal's own form on the day it was written, where Status has two values and Area five and both are Selects among ten fields. The rule was wrong, not the form.

rules.title: A switch applies, a checkbox submits
rules.because: They look interchangeable and are not: a switch promises the change already happened, a checkbox promises it happens when the form is saved. Getting it the wrong way round produces either a setting nobody realises they have to save, or a form that changes something before the reader agreed to it. The screen knows which it is; the spec says so, and the component follows.

rules.title: A slider is for a position, never for a figure
rules.because: A track answers "more or less" well and "how much exactly" badly: it cannot be typed, it cannot be pasted, and on a phone it cannot be landed on a value. So it is for the case where the exact number does not matter, and even then it owes a readout — a slider whose value is only its handle position is a control the reader cannot check.

rules.title: A capped text field says what is left
rules.because: A limit the reader meets by being cut off is a limit the screen kept to itself. <CharacterCount> is the one place this is said, and it says it as it is typed rather than on submit.

hard.because: Yes and No in a menu is a two-click answer to a one-click question, and it hides the current state behind a press.

A date assembled from three menus is three chances to build a day that does not exist, and a date typed into a plain field is a format argument with the reader. <DatePicker> takes both a keyboard and a calendar.
A password in a plain field is readable over a shoulder and offered to the browser as an ordinary value. This one is not a matter of taste.
A radio group is exactly one answer, by definition and by keyboard. Using it where several are allowed leaves the reader unable to express the answer at all.

notes.if: the options have no natural order
notes.say: alphabetical, and the same order every time the screen renders — a list that reshuffles is a list nobody learns
mark the OPTIONAL ones instead: marking the majority is noise, and the reader reads neither
attach it to the field with <InputGroup>, and repeat it wherever the value is read back
required only while it is shown — a hidden field that blocks submission is an error with nothing to point at

doc.$componentsNote: Every component named above is in the registry and is built. This layer was written on 2026-08-31 after an audit measured that eight input controls existed which no rule and no product ever named: DatePicker, DateRangePicker, Slider, RangeSlider, TagInput, CodeInput, InputGroup and ConditionalReveal. They were not unused because they were wrong; they were unused because nothing could say when to reach for them.

layers.means: Which kind of table, once the answer is a table

doc.$comment: The table decision layer. selection-rules.json answers WHICH REPRESENTATION a collection gets; card-rules.json answers WHICH CARD once the answer is cards; form-rules.json answers WHICH FORM once the zone takes input. This file answers the one that was left: once the answer is a table, WHICH KIND of table. A worklist, a comparison matrix, a spreadsheet and a totals report are four different objects that all render as rows and columns, and the system used to offer one component for all four. A kind is chosen by four questions and nothing else: what a row IS (rowUnit and axes), what the reader DOES with it (the same task verbs), HOW MANY rows there are (cardinality), and whether a CELL INTERACTS (editable, select, cells). Consolidated 2026-08-23 from SAP Fiori (responsive / grid / analytical / tree table and the thresholds between them), IBM Carbon (variants, row sizes, toolbar and batch action bar, expansion, skeleton), NN/g (the four user tasks with data tables, frozen headers, editing without a modal), Pencil and Paper (enterprise table patterns), uxpatterns.dev, Shopify Polaris (index table), Smashing Magazine (responsive and comparison tables), W3C WAI-ARIA APG (table, grid, treegrid) and WCAG 2.2 (1.3.1, 2.1.1, 2.5.8). The survey behind it is docs/RESEARCH-TABLES.md. check-screen-spec.mjs enforces it: a zone whose representation is a table or a grid must say which kind it is, and may only use a kind some matching rule chooses. Three craft rules hold for EVERY kind and are therefore not notes (a note that fires on every zone is noise): every table carries its own name (a caption, or an aria-label where the heading above already says the words); a table wide enough to scroll sideways freezes its first column, because a reader whose identifier scrolled away is on an unnamed row; and a table owes three states, not one — nothing yet, nothing matches, and loading.

record.means: A thing with fields of its own: an invoice, a user, a team.
record.test: The row has an id and a page it could be opened on.

fact.means: A stated value in a reference: a rate, a limit, a definition.
fact.test: Nobody acts on the row; they look it up and leave.

field.means: One attribute of ONE record, read top to bottom.
field.test: There is only one record on the screen, so nothing is compared across rows.

attribute.means: A property compared across a few subjects that are the COLUMNS.
attribute.test: Turning the table on its side would give one row per subject, and there are only a handful of them.

crossing.means: The cell where two categorical axes meet.
crossing.test: A value is identified by both of its headers, not by its row.

event.means: Something that happened at a time, appended to a stream.
event.test: The newest row is at one end and the set only grows.

change.means: A difference between two versions of the same thing.
change.test: The row has a before and an after.

resource.means: Something booked or scheduled against time.
resource.test: The reader is looking for a gap rather than for a total.

rows.means: One axis: the columns are fields of the row.

cross.means: Two axes: the columns are a second category, and the cell is a measure.

static.means: Nothing in a cell is operated. The ARIA role is `table`.
static.owes: Nothing beyond the table's own name and header scopes.

interactive.means: Cells are focused, typed into or walked. The ARIA role is `grid` (or `treegrid` with hierarchy).
interactive.owes: One tab stop for the whole widget, arrow keys between cells, Home and End. A grid role with no keyboard is worse than a plain table.

none.means: Rows are read and acted on one at a time.

single.means: One row at a time is picked, usually to open it.

batch.means: Several rows are picked and ONE action is applied to all of them.

grouped.means: Rows fall into named sets the reader can collapse.

hierarchy.means: Rows contain rows: the nesting is part of the data.

reference.means: A static table of stated values: rates, limits, a glossary of levels.
reference.useWhen: The rows are looked up and left. No sorting, no selection, no pager.
reference.notWhen: The reader has to find one row among many, which is a list table.
owes: A caption or an aria-label: a reference nobody can name is a reference nobody can cite.

list.means: Find and act: the table a collection screen is built around.
list.useWhen: Filters and a search narrow it, columns sort it, the first column opens the record.
list.notWhen: The queue is given and nobody goes looking, which is a worklist.
owes: A default sort that answers 'what would I look at first'.
An empty state for nothing-yet and a different one for nothing-matches.

worklist.means: A given queue where every row needs a decision or a completion.
worklist.useWhen: The set arrives already narrowed: status, one action per row, and the reading order IS the priority order.
worklist.notWhen: The user still has to find the rows first, which is a list table.
owes: Static headers: a sortable column hands back the ranking the screen decided.
One action per row, in the last column, always visible.

selection.means: Picking N rows and applying one action to all of them.
selection.useWhen: The job is the selection: a checkbox column, a tri-state select all, and a bar that names the count.
selection.notWhen: Only one row is ever acted on, which is a row action rather than a batch.
owes: The header checkbox is indeterminate when some rows are picked, never off.
A selection that can reach past the page says so in words ('Select all 1,284').
A destructive batch action confirms and names the number.

editable-grid.means: A spreadsheet: editing across records is the primary task.
editable-grid.useWhen: Cells are focused and typed over, and each commits on its own.
editable-grid.notWhen: One record at a time, which is a form, or occasional edits on a table, which are a row action.
owes: Editing is entered deliberately (Enter, F2 or a double click), never on a stray click.
The editor looks different from the value it replaced.
The grid keyboard model, in full: one tab stop, arrows, Home and End.

virtualized.means: A windowed table: thousands of rows, only the visible ones in the DOM.
virtualized.useWhen: The row count is unbounded or large enough that a page of them is not the unit.
virtualized.notWhen: Fewer rows than one page holds: the machinery costs more than it saves.
owes: A fixed row height, which is what the windowing is built on.
The keyboard moving the WINDOW, not only the focus: a row the arrow key reaches has to exist.

tree.means: Hierarchy with columns: a bill of materials, an org rollup, a folder tree with size and owner.
tree.useWhen: The nesting is part of the data and the values matter at every level.
tree.notWhen: The hierarchy has no columns, which is `Tree`; or the rows are siblings, which is a table.
owes: role=treegrid, and the keyboard that goes with it: Right opens or steps in, Left closes or steps out.
aria-level, aria-posinset and aria-setsize on every row.

grouped.means: Rows under named headings the reader can collapse.
grouped.useWhen: The set falls into groups that are part of the data: by owner, by status, by month.
grouped.notWhen: The grouping is really a filter the reader changes, which is a filter.
owes: A collapsed group still says its name and how many rows it is holding.

expandable.means: A row with a second layer, revealed in place.
expandable.useWhen: Most readers need six columns and a few need the twentieth field, and the page must not change under them.
expandable.notWhen: Everyone needs the detail, which means the columns are wrong.
owes: aria-expanded on the disclosure, and a name that says WHICH row it opens.
The detail row spans every column, including the checkbox and disclosure cells.

analytical.means: Transactions under a total: subtotals, a totals row, a drill from the sum to the rows.
analytical.useWhen: Aggregation is the point, and the aggregate is read as often as the rows.
analytical.notWhen: Nothing is summed, so a footer would say nothing.
owes: The total lives in TFoot, not in a body row: a total that scrolls away is a total nobody reads.
Money and counts end-aligned, on tabular figures, units named once in the header.

pivot.means: Two categorical axes and one measure in the cell.
pivot.useWhen: Teams by month, region by product, skill by level: the reader is looking at a crossing.
pivot.notWhen: One axis, which is a plain table with a sortable column.
owes: Both headers scoped: a cell belongs to a row AND a column.
No observation is written as such, never as a zero.

comparison.means: A few subjects as COLUMNS and their attributes as rows.
comparison.useWhen: Plans, vendors, candidates, options: three to five things compared across many properties.
comparison.notWhen: Many subjects: past about five, the subjects are records and belong in rows.
owes: A tick carries its own words: colour and shape are the shorthand, the text is the fact.
The recommended column is marked down its whole length, not on the header alone.

key-value.means: One record's fields, read top to bottom.
key-value.useWhen: There is exactly one record on the screen, so nothing is compared across rows.
key-value.notWhen: More than one record, which is columns.
owes: A real description list, so a screen reader hears field and value as a pair.

schedule.means: A resource against time: rooms by hour, people by day, machines by week.
schedule.useWhen: The reader is looking for a gap or for a clash.
schedule.notWhen: A single date is being picked, which is `Calendar`.
owes: The resource column frozen: a schedule scrolled sideways belongs to nobody.
A free slot says it is free rather than being an empty box.

heatmap.means: A matrix read as a pattern: the shape across the grid matters more than any one number.
heatmap.useWhen: Density, coverage, adoption: the reader is looking for where it is hot.
heatmap.notWhen: The exact values are read, where the colour becomes decoration over the number.
owes: The ramp is discrete and scaled to the largest observation in the table.
The number stays in the cell: a colour without its value is a picture, not a table.

bar-in-cell.means: A ranking read at a glance: the number and its length in the same cell.
bar-in-cell.useWhen: The rows are comparable on one scale and the order is the point.
bar-in-cell.notWhen: The numbers are not on one scale, where a bar compares nothing.
owes: One scale for every bar in the column, stated in the header.

log.means: A dense append-only stream: time first, payload after it.
log.useWhen: Events are scanned and filtered rather than sorted, and the set only grows.
log.notWhen: The events are read one at a time, which is a timeline.
owes: Compact density and one line per event: a wrapped payload turns a log into a wall.
Filtering, not sorting: the order is the clock.

diff.means: Before and after, side by side: an audit trail, a review of an edit.
diff.useWhen: The row is a change rather than a record.
diff.notWhen: Only the current value matters, which is a plain table.
owes: Added, removed and changed said in words as well as in colour.

card-table.means: The top rows inside a card on an overview, with no table chrome.
card-table.useWhen: A glance at what is in a collection, with the whole card linking onward.
card-table.notWhen: The reader acts on the rows here, which needs a real table with its toolbar.
owes: No pager, no filters, no sort: the card is a glance and the link is the way in.
A row count or a 'see all' so the reader knows this is the top of something.

ticks.means: Binary coverage across a set: supported or not.
ticks.useWhen: Every cell is a yes or a no, and the pattern of yeses is the answer.
ticks.notWhen: The cell holds a value rather than a yes or a no, which is a comparison or a pivot.
owes: The tick and the blank both carry their words for anyone not reading the shape.

rules.title: Looked-up values are a reference table
rules.because: A table nobody acts on owes no chrome: sorting, selection and a pager on a rate card are controls with nothing behind them (Fiori: a display table is not a list report). Records that are only READ land here too, which is what a detail page's small table and an overview card's top five are.
rules.good: <Table size="sm"> of levels and their thresholds, captioned
rules.bad: a rate card with sortable headers and a Load more

rules.title: Find and act is a list table
rules.because: Finding is narrowing then choosing: filters, a search, a default sort that answers 'what first', and a first column that opens the record (NN/g: the four tasks).
rules.good: TableToolbar + FilterBar over a <Table> with a sortable header and Pagination
rules.bad: a table of 400 rows with no search, no filter and no total

rules.title: A given queue is a worklist
rules.because: The set is already narrowed, so the chrome that finds is dead weight and the reading order IS the priority order (Fiori worklist = list report minus the filter bar).
rules.good: <Table> of items with a status Badge and one action per row
rules.bad: a worklist with sortable columns, which un-decides what the screen decided

rules.title: Picking rows for one action is a selection table
rules.because: The moment one action applies to many rows, the count and the way out are part of the interface (Carbon batch action bar).
rules.good: checkbox column + tri-state header + <BatchActions count={3}>
rules.bad: an Export button beside a table with three rows ticked and no count anywhere

rules.title: Editing across records is a grid
rules.because: When cell-level editing is the primary task the surface is a data grid; a plain table carries occasional inline edits only (Smart Interface Design Patterns).
rules.good: <DataGrid> with editable columns and onCellChange
rules.bad: a table with an Edit dialog behind every cell

rules.title: An unbounded set is windowed
rules.because: A table renders a known number of rows; past a few thousand the browser is the bottleneck and the answer is windowing, not a taller page.
rules.good: <DataGrid rowHeight={40} height={480}>
rules.bad: a <Table> mapping 40,000 rows into the DOM

rules.title: Nesting with columns is a tree table
rules.because: Hierarchy plus values is the treegrid pattern: rows that contain rows, with the level announced rather than only indented (W3C APG).
rules.good: <TreeTable> with aria-level and Right/Left opening and closing
rules.bad: an indented <Table> where the nesting is a padding class

rules.title: Named sets are groups
rules.because: A group is part of the data, and a collapsed one still has to say what it is holding.
rules.good: TrGroup with the name and the count, over the rows it heads
rules.bad: a repeated value in the first column standing in for a heading

rules.title: A second layer belongs in the row
rules.because: Expansion presents a large amount of data in a small space without leaving the page (Carbon); the alternative is either twenty columns or a route change.
rules.good: TdExpand + TrDetail with the fields most readers do not need
rules.bad: a twentieth column nobody reads, or a modal over the table

rules.title: Aggregation earns a footer
rules.because: Analysis is one loop: the aggregate and the rows it came from, on one screen, acted on where they are (Fiori analytical list page).
rules.good: <TFoot> with the total, Stat row above the table
rules.bad: the total on another screen, or as the last body row

rules.title: Two axes are a matrix
rules.because: A cell identified by both of its headers is a crossing, not a field: the shape is a crosstab and both headers have to be scoped.
rules.good: <PivotTable rows={teams} columns={months} value={hours}>
rules.bad: a table with a column per month and a hand-built total row

rules.title: A few subjects are columns
rules.because: Three to five subjects across twenty properties reads down the column; the same data as rows reads as twenty tables (Smashing: feature comparison tables).
rules.good: <ComparisonTable subjects={plans} rows={features}>
rules.bad: three <Card>s the reader has to hold in their head to compare

rules.title: One record is a description list
rules.because: With one record there is nothing to compare across rows, and a two-column table of labels is a description list wearing a grid (NN/g).
rules.good: <Descriptions items={fields}>
rules.bad: a two-column <Table> whose header row says Field and Value

rules.title: A stream is a log
rules.because: An append-only set is scanned and filtered rather than sorted: the order is the clock, and density is what makes it readable.
rules.good: <Table size="sm" nowrap> with the time first and a search over it
rules.bad: a log with sortable columns and 56px rows

rules.title: A before and an after is a diff
rules.because: A change has two values of one field; two columns of the same field at two times is the only shape that shows it.
rules.good: <DiffTable changes={changes}>
rules.bad: two tables side by side and the reader doing the comparing

rules.title: A resource against time is a schedule
rules.because: Time on one axis and the resource on the other is what makes a gap visible; a list of bookings hides exactly the thing being looked for.
rules.good: <ScheduleGrid resources={rooms} slots={hours}>
rules.bad: a list of bookings sorted by start time

rules.title: A glance inside a card is a card table
rules.because: An overview card shows the top of a collection and links onward; the chrome of a real table would outweigh three rows (Fiori overview page, table card).
rules.good: <Card flush> with a five-row <Table> and a link to all of them
rules.bad: a card with a pager, a filter bar and four rows

hard.because: <Table> renders every row it is given; an unbounded set has to be windowed (AGENTS.md: choosing between neighbours).
Editing as the primary task needs cells that take focus, which is the grid pattern and not a table with inputs in it.
