A batch action needs a count, a select-all and a way out; a reference table and a card glance have nowhere to put them.
Interactive cells make the widget a grid, which owes a keyboard model a static reference table does not have.

notes.say: hundreds of rows need a pager with the total (Pagination) or a LoadMore: the total is orientation, and without it a filtered table and a small table look identical.
three states, not one: empty because nothing exists yet, empty because the filters match nothing, and loading. TableEmpty and TableSkeleton are the parts.
a comparison table holds three to five subjects: past that the columns run out, and the subjects are records that belong in rows.
the number stays in the cell. A ramp with the values taken out is a picture of the data, and the reader cannot get back to the number they came for.
interactive cells make this a grid, and the grid pattern is a contract: one tab stop, arrow keys between cells, Home and End. DataGrid implements it; a hand-rolled table with inputs in it does not.

doc.$componentsNote: Every component named above is in the registry and is built. Sub-parts of Table (TFoot, TrGroup, TdExpand, TrDetail, TableEmpty, TableSkeleton) are named in `owes` rather than in `components`, because the registry lists the component and the spec names the component: a zone says <Table>, and the parts it owes are what the review checks.

layers.means: What one column carries, and what that decides

doc.$comment: The layer under table-rules.json. That file answers WHICH TABLE a zone gets; this one answers what a COLUMN is made of. A column carries one kind of value for every row (a column that is a badge on some rows and a sentence on others is two columns), and the kind decides four things nobody should have to argue about again: which way it aligns, whether its width is fixed or flexible, whether it may be sorted, and what it owes. Consolidated 2026-08-23 from Handsontable's data-table anatomy (cell variants and states), setproduct's 2026 guide (cell content patterns, the fixed-plus-flexible width hybrid), PatternFly (truncation: four characters, never a header, the tooltip), Carbon (row height, toolbar, expansion), SAP Fiori (smart-table columns, micro charts in a cell, amount and currency together), NN/g (the four user tasks) and Pencil and Paper. The survey behind it is docs/RESEARCH-TABLE-CONTENT.md. check-screen-spec.mjs enforces it: a table zone that declares its columns is held to these rules, column by column.

identifier.means: The record's own name or number: what the row IS.
identifier.useWhen: Always. Every table has exactly one, and it is the first column.
owes: First column, and a row header (scope="row") so a screen reader can say which record a value belongs to.
Human-readable: a UUID is not an identifier a person can use.
It is the link to the record, if the record has a page.

identity.means: A person or a team as the value of a column.
identity.useWhen: The column answers 'who': an owner, an assignee, a requester.
identity.notWhen: Only a name is shown and no face is available — that is a text column.
owes: The face beside the name, never above it.
Several people are an AvatarGroup with a +N, not five faces in a row.

text.means: A short value read as a word: a supplier, a place, a category.
text.useWhen: The value is read, not compared as a quantity.
text.notWhen: The value is a sentence: a column of sentences is a column that aligns nothing.
owes: One line, cut with an ellipsis, the whole value in a tooltip.

number.useWhen: The values are compared down the column.
number.notWhen: The digits are an identifier (an order number, a postcode): that reads as a word and starts.
owes: Tabular figures, which Td align="end" brings.
The unit in the header, once, not in every cell.

money.notWhen: A mixed-currency column where the codes differ per row still ends, but the code goes in the CELL (Fiori).
owes: One writing of an amount per system (lib/formatNumber money).
The currency in the header when the column is one currency.

percent.means: A share, a rate, a completion.
percent.useWhen: The value is a ratio the reader compares.
percent.notWhen: The share is the point and the number is not: that is a measure, with a bar.
owes: One decimal at most, and the same number of decimals down the column.

date.useWhen: A due date, a created date, a period.
date.notWhen: The reader thinks in 'how long ago', which is relative time.
owes: One format for the whole table.
A date is read as a word, so it starts even though it is digits.

relative-time.useWhen: A stream, an activity log, a 'last seen' column.
relative-time.notWhen: The exact moment matters (an audit, a schedule) — that is a date.
owes: The exact timestamp underneath, which Time already carries.

status.means: Which state a record is in.
status.useWhen: A workflow state, an outcome, a health.
status.notWhen: The value is free text — a status is a closed set or it is not a status.
owes: One word, one tone per state, and the word carries it: colour alone is not information.
Sorted in the order the workflow runs, never alphabetically.

tags.notWhen: There is exactly one, which is a status or a text column.
owes: Two visible plus a counted overflow that names the rest: a wrapped wall of pills makes every row a different height.

boolean.means: Supported or not, included or not.
boolean.useWhen: The column is a yes or a no for every row.
boolean.notWhen: There is a third state (unknown, partial) — that is a status.
owes: A tick and a blank, each carrying its words for anyone not reading the shape.

measure.means: A value on a scale, compared down the column.
measure.useWhen: The reader asks 'how much of it', not 'what is the number'.
measure.notWhen: The exact value is what is read: that is a number.
owes: The bar and the number in one cell.
One scale for the whole column, named in the header.

trend.means: The shape of a value over time.
trend.notWhen: The reader needs the values: that is a chart, on its own surface.
owes: No axes, no tooltip, no legend: a sparkline that needs a legend is a chart in the wrong place.

media.means: A picture that identifies the row.
media.useWhen: A product, a document, a recording.
media.notWhen: The picture IS the content and the row is a card — that is a card, not a table.
owes: A fixed box, so the image never drives the row height.

link.means: A record that lives somewhere else.
link.useWhen: The row points at a related thing: a supplier, a parent order, a ticket.
link.notWhen: It points at ITSELF — that is the identifier, which is already the link.
owes: The value is the link. A column of 'View' verbs is a column with no data in it.

actions.means: What can be done to this row.
actions.useWhen: Rows are acted on one at a time.
actions.notWhen: One action applies to many rows: that is a selection table and a batch bar.
owes: Last column, aligned to the end.
Under three actions are icon buttons with tooltips; more go in a menu.
Always visible: an action revealed on hover does not exist on a touch screen.

select.means: The checkbox that picks the row.
select.useWhen: The table is a selection table.
owes: First column, before the identifier.
A tri-state header checkbox, never a two-state one.

empty.useWhen: Any column whose value can be absent.
empty.notWhen: Never a kind of its own in a spec: it is what every other kind owes.
owes: 'None', 'Not set' or '0' — no value and zero are not the same fact, and a blank cell reads as a rendering failure.

rules.title: The identifier is first, and it is a row header
rules.because: A screen reader says the row header with every value in the row; a table whose first column is not the record's name is a grid of numbers belonging to nobody (NN/g: the human-readable identifier first).

rules.title: Compared quantities end, read values start
rules.because: Digits compare by place value only when they line up, and tabular figures come with the end alignment. Dates, IDs and postcodes are digits that are READ, so they start.

rules.title: Actions are last and select is first
rules.because: The row is read from its name to what can be done about it. A verb in the middle of the data is a verb nobody finds twice.

rules.title: A column nobody compares does not sort
rules.because: A sortable header promises an order; a column of pictures, pills or buttons has none, and the promise costs a control in every header.

rules.title: One two-line column, and only one
rules.because: Two facts in one cell is what makes a row scannable at all (a name over its email); two columns doing it makes the row a paragraph.

hard.because: A column of sentences aligns nothing (selection-rules R7). The text belongs in an expandable row or on the record.
A badge pushed to the end of a wide column floats away from the value it describes.

notes.say: eight columns or more: turn columns off (ColumnPicker), freeze the identifier (Table stickyColumn) and put the long tail in an expandable row, in that order. A twenty-column table is usually a pivot that has not been written as one.
fix the predictable columns (status, date, actions, select) and let the text ones flex, with a minimum on each: a table whose every column is content-sized re-flows as the data changes.
a text column truncates with <Truncate>: one line, an ellipsis, the whole value in a tooltip. Wrapping is for the one description column a table is allowed, and three lines is a paragraph.
the currency goes in the header when the column is one currency, and in the cell when the rows differ (Fiori). Not both.

doc.$componentsNote: Every component named above is in the registry and is built. Truncate, CellStack, TagGroup and Thumbnail were built with this file on 2026-08-23; the rest already existed and were only waiting to be told which column they belong in.

layers.means: Which regions a page archetype has, and what shape its body takes

doc.$comment: The GEOMETRY layer of the screen decision. selection-rules.json answers which representation a collection gets and card-rules.json answers which card; this file answers what SHAPE the page itself is: which regions it has, which it may not have, and what each may carry. It is the data behind <Page>, and it is the reason a new page type is an entry here rather than a new React file. check-screen-spec.mjs enforces it and checks it against the registry, so a preset built from a component the system does not have cannot sit here unnoticed. Sources and the measurements behind every choice: docs/RESEARCH-SCREENS.md (2026-08-23).

notices.means: Page-level messages above everything: a degraded service, a pending action, a banner the whole screen is qualified by.
notices.notFor: a message about one field or one row, which belongs beside it

header.means: The page's identity and its page-level actions.
header.notFor: filters and search, which narrow the content and belong in the toolbar

subnav.means: Navigation WITHIN the page: sections of one record, views of one collection.
subnav.notFor: moving between pages, which is the shell's nav

toolbar.means: What acts on the body as a whole: search, filters, batch actions, the view switcher.
toolbar.notFor: an action on one item, which belongs on that item

body.means: The content. Its shape is the page's geometry.

detail.means: The second pane of a list-detail body: what the current selection is.

aside.means: A supporting pane beside the body: reference the reader glances at without leaving the main task.
aside.notFor: the record itself, which is the body, or a selection's detail, which is the list-detail shape

footerBar.means: A sticky bar at the bottom carrying the commitment: submit, next, apply.
footerBar.notFor: an action that does not commit the page, which belongs in the header

single.means: One column of sections. The default, and right whenever the page has one subject.
single.source: the shape eight of the nine existing templates already are

list-detail.means: Two panes, selection-driven: the list on one side, the selected item on the other. Below the split floor the panes stack and one shows at a time.
list-detail.source: Material 3 canonical layout; SAP Fiori flexible column layout, which HOSTS floorplans rather than being one
rules: never instead of a details page in the information architecture: this is for identifying, monitoring and comparing while browsing, not for analysing one record (Cloudscape)
the detail pane shows an empty state when nothing is selected

feed.opensWhen: Opens when a page body IS a grid of equivalent items and does not hand its own grid in. The overview and the hub both looked like this and both turned out not to be.
feed.means: A responsive grid of equivalent items, browsed rather than searched.
feed.source: Material 3 canonical layout; the shape OverviewPageTemplate's board and the hub screens already are

board.opensWhen: Opens when the workshops board is rebuilt on a page block; it is 1,806 hand-rolled lines today.
board.means: Columns of movable items, where the column an item sits in IS its state.
board.source: one live case in this repository, hand-rolled in 1,806 lines

canvas.opensWhen: Opens with the first full-bleed body that manages its own space. Declared now so that escape is inside the system rather than out of it.
canvas.means: Free-form full-bleed content that manages its own space: a map, a diagram, an editor surface.
canvas.source: not in any canon; declared here so the escape from the system is still inside it

narrow.means: One short column, centred: a status page, a sign-in.
narrow.source: SystemPageTemplate arrived at 38rem on its own

reading.means: A column read line by line: a form, a settings page.
reading.source: FormPageTemplate and SettingsPageTemplate independently arrived at 52rem

default.means: The product width every other page uses, aligned with the header above it.

full.means: Edge to edge, for a body that manages its own space (canvas, board).

overview.why: Read at a glance and acted on elsewhere. A toolbar would mean the reader has to narrow something first, which is the list archetype.
overview.whyNotFeed: The page is not one grid: it is priority bands read top to bottom (context, then what is read first, then the board, then the widget grid), and only the last of those is a feed. `feed` describes a body that IS a grid of equivalent items, which is the hub. Corrected on 2026-08-23 against the shipped template.

list.why: Find and act. The toolbar is where the narrowing lives; the empty state is not optional because a list that can filter can always be filtered to nothing.

worklist.why: The queue is given. A FilterBar means the user still has to find, which is the list archetype (Fiori: worklist = list report minus the filter bar).

analytical.why: One investigation loop: the aggregate on top, the rows it summarises under it, acted on where they are (Fiori analytical list page).

detail.why: One record in full. The subnav is the tabs variant six screens hand-roll today; the aside is the supporting pane.
detail.whyItTookTwo: The first attempt on 2026-08-23 was reverted and the second landed the same day. Two things blocked it and both were real. (1) The panelled variant's CSS was written against a THREE-element structure where the page wrapper IS the two-column row; <Page> has four, so `.detail-page[data-panels] > *` and its neighbours would have selected the wrong element. Each of those rules was paid for by a bug, so they were re-pointed at Page's regions one at a time rather than swept. (2) The COLLAPSED aside is a rail one control wide and Page's aside region is `flex: 1 1 20rem`, so the rail would have become the panel again without the panel. Fixed by giving <Page> an `asideWidth` of `default | rail`: the block keeps the state, the page keeps the geometry, and neither learns the other's job.

hub.why: The items are destinations, not records: one tile per place, saying what waits inside it.
hub.whyNotFeed: The tiles are the CALLER's grid, handed in with the ref that measures whether they fit on one screen. The page lays out a column that holds a notice and then whatever the caller built; it does not own the track. Corrected on 2026-08-23 against the shipped template.

form.why: A capture, read line by line. Which KIND of form is the next decision down and form-rules.json computes it.
form.whyNotReading: The width that matters here is the COLUMN OF FIELDS, not the page: a page-sized form is a surface being filled in, and capping the surface at 52rem left a narrow white strip in the middle of an empty page. The reading cap sits on the fields inside the card. Corrected on 2026-08-23 against the shipped template, which had already learned this.

wizard.why: One step at a time with the stepper above and the commitment below. The footer bar is required: a wizard whose Next is somewhere else is not a wizard.
wizard.whyNotReading: The same correction the `form` archetype took on 2026-08-23, and for the same reason: the width that matters is the COLUMN OF FIELDS, not the page. A wizard is a form cut into steps, so capping the SURFACE at 52rem left a narrow white strip in the middle of an empty page with the stepper squeezed into it. The reading cap sits on the step column inside the card. Corrected on 2026-08-30, after the owner read it off the gallery.

settings.why: Grouped sections of explained knobs, found by scanning labels rather than by searching. No toolbar, for that reason.

auth.why: Minimal distraction. An auth page that also announces or navigates is two screens.
auth.whyNotPage: It is not a page INSIDE the shell, it is a root that replaces it: full viewport height, its own background, no app navigation. <Page> lays out a region of the shell, so expressing this through it would mean giving Page a way to not be in a shell, which is a second component wearing the first one's name. Found by the acceptance test on 2026-08-23.

system.why: Not found, unavailable, something broke. One short centred column with the way out. The name `system` names nothing and `status` would name the job (GOV.UK), but the rename belongs to the naming pass and has to happen everywhere at once; until then this key matches selection-rules.json, because two files with two names for one archetype is the rot the cross-checks exist to stop.

layers.means: What the screen does to the resource

doc.$comment: The LIFECYCLE axis. selection-rules.json answers what SHAPE a collection takes, page-rules.json what shape the page takes, card-rules.json which card, form-rules.json which form. All four ask what the screen LOOKS like. This one asks what it DOES to the resource — create, read, update, delete — and decides the three things that hang off that question and were decided by taste until now: which variant of a detail page, which shape an edit takes, and how hard a destruction is to confirm. Sources: AWS Cloudscape's resource-management patterns (the lifecycle taxonomy itself, the three details pages, the three edits and the three deletes), NN/g on destructive actions and undo. Measured against the registry on 2026-08-23; the audit is in docs/RESEARCH-SCREENS.md section 8.5.

create.means: The resource does not exist yet and the screen brings it into being.
create.decidedBy: form-rules.json — which KIND of form the capture is

read.means: The resource exists and the screen shows it: a collection to find in, or one record in full.
read.decidedBy: selection-rules.json for the collection, detailVariants below for the record

update.means: The resource exists and the screen changes it. Not the same question as create: the values are already there, and the smallest correct edit is often not a form at all.
update.decidedBy: editKinds below, then form-rules.json once the answer is a form

delete.means: The resource stops existing. The only stage whose mistake cannot be undone by doing it again.

plain.means: One record read top to bottom: sections in a column, reference in the aside.

tabs.means: One record with sections too long to stack: the sections become tabs and only one is on screen.
tabs.note: Six screens across the products hand-roll this today by putting <Tabs> in the body. The region exists on <Page> (`subnav`); what was missing was the rule saying when it is earned.

hub.means: A record whose job is to route onward: the page names what it is and then hands over to the places you act.

detailRules.title: Sections that fit stay stacked
detailRules.because: Tabs hide content behind a click and cost a page's worth of scanning; under about four sections the whole record is cheaper to read at once (Cloudscape details page).
detailRules.bad: four tabs with two fields behind each

detailRules.title: Too many sections to stack becomes tabs
detailRules.because: Past roughly five sections the page stops being readable in one pass and the reader is scrolling to navigate. Tabs turn that scrolling back into a choice (Cloudscape details page with tabs).

detailRules.title: A record that is a doorway is a hub
detailRules.because: When nothing is decided on the record itself and every action lives on another screen, the page's job is to say what is inside each door (Cloudscape details page as a hub).
detailRules.bad: a details page whose every section ends in a link

attribute.means: One value, changed where it is read: click it, type, commit on blur.
attribute.builtBecause: InlineText is the part this was waiting for, and it was already in the registry: the SAME element becomes editable on click, Enter commits, Escape reverts, blur saves — which is this kind, word for word. The record asked for "an InlineEdit component" and the system built one under another name, so the status outlived the gap it described (found 2026-08-27, the same way four form kinds were found on 2026-08-26). `Input` was never right here: a control with its own chrome is the thing this kind exists NOT to be.

inline.means: A row edited in its own place in the collection, the rest of the rows staying put.
inline.note: DataGrid's editable cells are this kind at collection scale; selection-rules R2 and H2 already send editing-as-the-primary-task here.

page.means: The whole record edited at once, on its own screen or in its own dialog.
page.note: Which kind of form it then is, is form-rules.json's decision, not this one.

editRules.title: One value is not a form
editRules.because: Opening a dialog to change one value costs two clicks and a context switch for a change the reader was already looking at (Cloudscape attribute editing).
editRules.bad: an Edit button that opens a modal with a single Input

editRules.title: Editing across rows is a grid
editRules.because: When the work is changing the same field on many records, a dialog per record is the whole task done the slow way (Smart Interface Design Patterns).
editRules.bad: an Edit dialog behind every row

editRules.title: Changing the record is a form
editRules.because: Several fields committed together need one submit, one error summary and one unsaved-changes guard, which is what the form layer already owns.

undo.means: It just happens, and a Toast offers the way back for as long as it is on screen.
undo.note: Toast carries `action: { label, onAction }`, so this kind is buildable today and nothing in the products uses it yet.

confirm.means: A yes/no dialog naming the thing and what goes with it.

confirm-typed.means: A dialog that will not arm its button until the reader types the resource's name.
confirm-typed.note: Unblocked on 2026-08-26 by folding <FormModal> and <ConfirmDialog> into <Modal>. The blocker was that one dialog took input and the other coloured its commitment, and no dialog did both; one Modal with `children` and `actions.tone` does. Arm it with `actions.confirmDisabled` until the typed name matches.

deleteRules.title: Reversible destruction needs no dialog
deleteRules.because: A confirmation that guards something reversible trains the reader to click through confirmations, which is how the unreversible one gets clicked through too (NN/g).
deleteRules.good: the row goes, a Toast says "Deleted. Undo"
deleteRules.bad: "Are you sure?" for removing a filter chip

deleteRules.title: The ordinary case is a yes/no
deleteRules.because: One record, gone for good: the reader needs to see WHICH record and what goes with it, and then say yes once.
deleteRules.good: <Modal size="sm" actions={{ tone: 'destructive' }}> naming the record

deleteRules.title: Destruction that reaches other people is typed
deleteRules.because: When the act removes other people's work, or a container with things inside it, the cost of a mis-click is not the reader's alone. Typing the name is the one guard that a habitual clicker cannot do by reflex (Cloudscape delete with additional confirmation).
deleteRules.bad: the same Are-you-sure that deletes one row also deletes the workspace

hard.because: An undo affordance for something that cannot be undone is a lie in the interface.
